newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia rail workers strike, government stands firm.
newsitem.headline: Croatia rail workers strike, government stands firm.

text.p: Striking Croatian railway workers paralysed rail traffic across the country on Friday for the second day to press demands for higher wages and better working conditions, but the government said it was standing firm.

Some 11,000 workers of the loss-making Croatian state railways (HZ) defied management pleas to end the strike, which halted nearly 80 percent of services, but the government refused to negotiate their demands, saying they had no basis.
"The losses caused by the strike are huge, but they are to be blamed on the government which refuses to negotiate," Zlatko Pavletic, the rail workers' union leader, told the state news agency HINA.
HZ director Marijan Klaric told state radio: "In this way we are directly damaging the entire Croatian economy and the railworkers. We are reducing the HZ profits, which are minimal anyway".

The railway workers' union responded by threatening to bring all railway traffic to a standstill. Strikers said they were running a reduced service of international and cargo trains, and about 20 percent of passenger trains.
"If the pressure continues we'll suspend this minimum traffic as well," Pavletic said.
Transport Minister Zeljko Luzavec ordered more domestic trains to resume service and the HZ threatened to sack all workers failing to obey the order.
Klaric later said that strikers were threatening railmen willing to return to work. He said the rail network would be completely paralysed by the strike on Saturday.

A HZ statement issued on Friday evening called on the strikers " to duly and seriously consider the gravity of the situation if they want to prevent the application of measures protecting the country's vital interests".

Croatia's top political body, the Council for Defence and National Security (VONS), convened on Friday and extended its support to the government, which is facing unprecedented waves of poverty-driven protests.

"The government has done everything it could to improve the status of railway workers," VONS said in a statement carried by HINA. It also said that some railway employees had higher wages than top government officials.
The Croatian parliament is due to discuss a restructuring of the loss-making railway company soon.
The rail strike follows a wave of protests in Croatia in the past week as pensioners, teachers and public sector workers have taken to the streets to demand pay and pension increases.
Living standards in the former Yugoslav republic have plunged since 1993, when the government launched a harsh stabilisation programme to curb hyperinflation.
